dimension_grades.evidence: The document has no TL;DR or summary section; it opens with background prose about distributed systems and the history of rate limiting, with no upfront statement of architectural decisions affecting callers.

Critical behaviors such as fail-open vs. fail-closed semantics, retry behavior, and what happens when Redis is unavailable are never mentioned anywhere in the document, let alone called out prominently.
There is no non-goals section anywhere in the document; the document only describes what the system will do, never what it explicitly will not do.

The API design and configuration model (Sections 6–7) appear after extensive historical context, philosophy, and architecture prose (Sections 1–5), burying caller-constraining decisions deep in the document.

grades.criterion_name: Code examples as primary entry points

dimension_grades.evidence: The only code shown is a protobuf service definition (server-side schema); there are no caller-side code examples in any programming language showing how to actually invoke the API.
No client library usage, middleware patterns, or production idioms are shown; the document contains only a protobuf definition and a YAML configuration example.
No code examples exist that demonstrate error handling; the document never shows what a caller should do when receiving OVER_LIMIT or when the service is unavailable.
Neither the protobuf definition nor the YAML configuration example contains any inline comments explaining the 'why' behind non-obvious lines.

grades.criterion_name: Concrete debugging artifacts in operational sections

dimension_grades.evidence: Section 10 (Security Considerations) mentions that unauthorized requests 'are rejected' but never provides the exact gRPC status code, error message, or response body a caller would see.
Failure modes are described from the system's internal perspective (e.g., 'the service applies its own internal rate limits') with no description of what a caller observes when failures occur.
Section 11 states metrics are 'exported in Prometheus format' and mentions a Grafana dashboard, but no specific metric names, structured log fields, or trace attributes are named anywhere.
Section 10 states unauthorized domain access 'are rejected' but provides no example of the rejected request, the gRPC status code returned, or the error message body.
Section 5 describes algorithm tradeoffs in neutral prose (e.g., fixed window 'boundary problem') but never explicitly flags any design decision as a tradeoff with a cost to callers.
No section identifies specific teams, use cases, or workflows that are negatively affected by any design decision made in this document.
While Section 2 mentions Envoy was considered and rejected, no workarounds or alternatives are offered for teams whose use cases are constrained by the chosen design decisions.
The document contains no admonition boxes, blockquotes, or visually distinct callout formatting of any kind throughout its entirety.
Section 5 compares three rate limiting algorithms entirely in prose paragraphs with no table, and Section 9 lists performance numbers in prose sentences rather than a table.
No bold or emphasized text appears anywhere in the document body; all key terms, decisions, and requirements are presented in plain prose.
Section 6 (API Design) references the domain concept without defining it, requiring readers to have read Section 7 or prior sections; sections rely on context established elsewhere.
No callout or admonition boxes are used anywhere in the document; warnings such as the fixed window boundary problem are embedded in plain prose paragraphs.
